venture.ventureIdea: MealMate is a campus-focused meal pre-ordering and subscription platform that connects students with university canteens and nearby food partners. Students can view menus, compare prices, pre-order meals, choose pickup slots, subscribe to affordable meal plans and rate food quality. Vendors receive consolidated demand forecasts, digital orders and basic inventory insights. Unlike a generic food-delivery app, MealMate is designed for high-frequency campus meals, faster pickup, student budgets and reduced food waste.

mission0.ventureIdea: MealMate is a campus-focused meal pre-ordering and subscription platform that connects students with university canteens and nearby food partners. Students can view menus, compare prices, pre-order meals, choose pickup slots, subscribe to affordable meal plans and rate food quality. Vendors receive consolidated demand forecasts, digital orders and basic inventory insights. Unlike a generic food-delivery app, MealMate is designed for high-frequency campus meals, faster pickup, student budgets and reduced food waste.
mission0.problemSolved: Students face long queues, uncertain menu availability, inconsistent pricing and last-minute meal decisions. Canteens and nearby food vendors lack reliable demand visibility, causing stock-outs, overproduction, slow service and avoidable food waste. General food-delivery platforms add delivery charges and commissions without solving the daily campus-meal problem.
mission0.initialCustomer: The initial users are DBS Global University students, especially hostel residents, day scholars and students with tightly scheduled classes. The initial paying business customers are campus canteens and nearby affordable food vendors seeking predictable demand, faster order handling and repeat purchases.
mission0.geography: DBS Global University campus and nearby Dehradun student and hostel clusters
mission0.whyChosen: Campus meals are a frequent and observable student problem. Queue time, uncertain availability, limited budgets and food waste can be measured directly through interviews and pilot transactions. The idea also supports a focused digital MVP that can be tested within one campus before expanding to other colleges.

frictions.whyWorkaroundUnsatisfactory: The workaround wastes time, provides no inventory certainty, adds delivery fees and may cause students to miss classes or settle for unsuitable meals.
frictions.evidenceSource: Working hypothesis based on commonly observable campus dining patterns; direct validation is pending.
frictions.whoExperiences: DBS Global University students, especially hostel residents and students with back-to-back classes.
frictions.whenOccurs: Lunch and dinner peaks, particularly between consecutive classes, examinations and event days.
frictions.currentWorkaround: Students visit the canteen physically, ask friends about availability, skip meals or order through general delivery apps.
frictions.friction: Students lose time in queues and still face uncertainty about whether preferred, affordable meals will be available when their classes end.
Students lack a convenient way to plan predictable, budget-controlled daily meals without repeatedly deciding and paying for each order.
frictions.whoExperiences: Hostel residents and price-sensitive students who purchase prepared meals several times per week.
frictions.whenOccurs: At the beginning of a week or month and during periods of heavy academic workload.
frictions.currentWorkaround: Students keep informal monthly arrangements with vendors, pay per meal or switch between canteens and delivery apps.
frictions.whyWorkaroundUnsatisfactory: Informal plans offer limited choice, weak service accountability, unclear savings and no simple pause, change or feedback mechanism.
frictions.evidenceSource: Founder assumption requiring interviews and willingness-to-pay testing with students.

frictions.friction: Campus food vendors cannot accurately forecast demand, resulting in stock-outs of popular dishes, surplus food, slow order handling and lost sales.
frictions.whoExperiences: University canteens and nearby affordable restaurants serving concentrated student demand.
frictions.whenOccurs: Meal preparation and peak service periods, especially when class schedules or campus events change demand.
frictions.currentWorkaround: Vendors rely on experience, rough estimates, WhatsApp messages and walk-in demand.
frictions.whyWorkaroundUnsatisfactory: Manual forecasting is inconsistent; vendors learn about demand only after preparation, while fragmented messages create errors and congestion.
frictions.evidenceSource: Business-side hypothesis requiring vendor interviews and a short pilot using pre-order data.

mission1.confidenceEvidenceNeeded: Survey at least 50 DGU students, observe lunch queues and stock-outs across five weekdays, interview at least three food vendors, and run a two-week pre-order pilot measuring wait-time reduction, fulfilment rate and repeat usage.

mission2.functionalJob: Secure an affordable meal that is available at a predictable time, without waiting in a queue or repeatedly checking multiple vendors.
mission2.emotionalJob: Feel confident and in control of daily meals, without the stress of running out of time, exceeding a student budget or discovering that preferred food is unavailable.
mission2.socialJob: Be seen as organised, punctual and capable of balancing academics, health and personal spending.

primaryJTBD.motivationAction: pre-order a suitable, affordable meal for a confirmed pickup time
primaryJTBD.desiredOutcome: I can eat on time, stay within budget and return to class without uncertainty or avoidable waiting
primaryJTBD.situation: my classes or academic commitments leave only a short meal break and campus outlets are likely to be crowded

mission2.addressedFriction: The JTBD directly addresses the primary friction by replacing uncertain walk-in availability and queues with advance menu visibility, order confirmation and scheduled pickup.

mission3.broadCustomerGroup: Higher-education students who regularly purchase prepared meals in and around university campuses
mission3.specificSegment: DBS Global University hostel residents and day scholars who buy at least four campus or nearby meals per week and frequently have short meal breaks
mission3.demographicsRole: Primarily 20–27-year-old undergraduate and postgraduate students; secondary buyer group: campus canteen operators and nearby food vendors
mission3.geography: DBS Global University campus and food outlets within an initial 2-km service radius in Dehradun
mission3.situationContext: Between classes, during lunch and dinner peaks, before examinations and on event days when students have limited time and outlets face concentrated demand
mission3.buyingBehaviour: Frequent ₹80–₹150 meal purchases, UPI-led payments, preference for visible value and convenience, and strong influence from classmates, reviews and WhatsApp recommendations
mission3.willingnessToPay: Students are expected to pay ₹80–₹150 per meal but should not face a separate booking fee; willingness to adopt depends on price parity, reliable fulfilment and time saved
mission3.reachStrategy: Class and hostel WhatsApp groups, cafeteria-table QR codes, student ambassadors, society partnerships, orientation events, campus posters and vendor counters
mission3.beachheadSegment: DGU students aged 20–27 who purchase at least four prepared meals per week and have meal breaks shorter than 45 minutes, beginning with hostel residents and first-year MBA cohorts

mission4.customerPain: Students waste limited meal breaks in queues and still face uncertain availability, inconsistent value and repeated decision-making.
mission4.desiredGain: A confirmed affordable meal, predictable pickup time, shorter waiting, clearer spending and fewer skipped or rushed meals.
mission4.productService: A campus-focused mobile platform for live menus, meal pre-orders, pickup slots, value bundles, subscriptions and vendor demand visibility
mission4.mainBenefit: Reliable meal access at campus prices with faster pickup and no separate student booking fee
mission4.reasonToBelieve: The model will be validated through one campus-canteen partnership, live inventory updates and a two-week pilot measuring order fulfilment, median pickup wait and repeat usage; these are planned proof points, not completed evidence.
mission4.cvpStatement: For time-constrained DGU students who struggle with queues and uncertain meal availability, MessMate provides campus-priced meal pre-ordering with confirmed pickup slots, so they can eat on time, control spending and return to class without avoidable waiting.
mission4.whyChooseOverDoingNothing: Doing nothing means repeatedly losing time, accepting stock-outs or paying more for delivery. MessMate requires only a short advance order while preserving familiar vendors and campus-level pricing.

mission7.priceEvidenceSource: Planning assumption: average meal value ₹120 and a 10% vendor commission produce approximately ₹12 platform revenue per fulfilled order. Validate through at least three vendor negotiations and a live price-parity pilot.
mission7.costEvidenceSource: Planning assumption: ₹3 variable cost per order for payment processing, notifications, rewards and support; ₹25,000 lean monthly fixed cost for technology, campus operations and merchant support. Supplier quotations are pending.

ambitious.notes: An official campus partnership, six or more outlets, strong ambassador adoption, repeat meal bundles and reliable pickup performance allow 800 active students to average twelve monthly orders.

base.notes: Three reliable outlets participate, QR and WhatsApp acquisition reaches the beachhead, fulfilment remains dependable and 350 active students average ten monthly orders.

conservative.notes: Only one outlet joins, awareness depends mainly on peer referrals, menus are updated manually and students continue using walk-in ordering. This produces 150 active customers completing six orders each per month.

mission8.totalCustomersEvidence: Planning estimate of 400,000 higher-education students in Uttarakhand. AISHE 2022–23 parliamentary data reports 214,265 female enrolments; the exact all-gender total and meal-purchasing proportion must be verified before investment decisions.
mission8.annualSpendEvidence: Derived from Mission 7 base economics: ₹12 platform revenue per order × 10 orders per active customer per month × 12 months = ₹1,440 annual platform revenue per active customer.
mission8.serviceableEvidence: Working estimate of 40,000 students across reachable Dehradun higher-education clusters. Replace with institution-wise enrolment and hostel data during validation.
mission8.obtainableEvidence: 4,200 obtainable customer accounts over 12 months, equivalent to the Mission 7 base trajectory of 350 active customers per month × 12. This is 10.5% of the assumed Dehradun SAM and requires phased expansion beyond DGU, six participating outlets and strong retention.
mission8.mostUrgentAssumption: The most urgent assumption is whether at least 350 students will complete ten orders per month while participating vendors accept an approximately 10% commission without raising student prices.

topAssumptions.evidenceNeeded: Timestamped order records showing first and repeat purchases, cohort repeat rate, orders per user, cancellations and pickup waiting time.
topAssumptions.assumption: At least 50 DGU students will place a campus-priced pre-order and at least 30% will order again within seven days.
topAssumptions.howToTest: Run a two-week pilot with 50 activated students across two outlets and expose all users to the same confirmed-pickup proposition.
topAssumptions.whyItMatters: If students do not repeat, projected order frequency, contribution revenue and customer-acquisition payback fail.

topAssumptions.evidenceNeeded: Written commercial terms, transaction settlements, menu-price comparisons, vendor margin feedback and continued participation after the pilot.
topAssumptions.assumption: Food vendors will accept an approximately 10% commission while maintaining price parity and reliable menu updates.
topAssumptions.howToTest: Negotiate with at least three vendors, secure two written pilot commitments and run real transactions at the proposed commission for two weeks.
topAssumptions.whyItMatters: Without sufficient commission and price parity, MessMate either lacks revenue or loses its student value advantage; without vendor participation, the marketplace has no supply.
Reliability is the core differentiation. Operational failure would recreate the same uncertainty and queues MessMate promises to remove.
topAssumptions.howToTest: Operate capped slots at two outlets during peak periods, audit inventory mismatches and compare promised versus actual ready and pickup times.
topAssumptions.evidenceNeeded: Timestamped preparation and pickup logs, fulfilment percentage, stock-out rate, median and 90th-percentile wait time, complaints and vendor workload observations.
topAssumptions.assumption: Outlet-confirmed inventory and capped pickup slots can achieve at least 90% fulfilment with a median pickup wait below seven minutes.
